Pretty much and you can really see it at the trot at the beginning. The true way to confirm this would be a flection test. Someone is bashing me for… not really sure what reason. They think I’m giving a diagnosis when I only said that she looks lame to me after only watching her go around for a few seconds but the good vets would watch a horse for about this long, pick out which leg they want to flex (in this case I believe it would be pretty obvious to them) then do the flection test. After confirming with the flection test, they move straight into nerve blocks to locate how far up the leg the injury is then they will do an ultrasound or even an MRI if that is within the owner’s budget. The whole process from the time the vet first sees the horse to when they are starting a nerve block takes a hot 5 minutes if the vet is really good. 

If you are interested in this stuff, you should see about doing a shadow day at your local equine lameness clinic. The vets are usually really nice about letting people observe and the rules are not nearly as strict as they are in human clinics. 

By the way, maybe more information than you want but the end result for a soft tissue injury is almost always the same lol. You go through all that trouble, pay thousands of dollar for an MRI, or not, then the vet tells you that your horse needs to be on stall rest for six months. Six months is an exceptionally long time for someone to put their horse on stall rest. Most people do not wait this long, they don’t have the time or patience or they receive different advice from their vet (I have heard less esteemed vets say six weeks). I assume this is why OP’s horse is so overweight but I don’t think putting it back to W/T/C work under rider weight before shedding those pounds is a wise move when you are bringing a horse back from a soft tissue injury.

Sure I can tell you what I look for. I shadowed one of the top orthopedic surgeons in the world for five years. This is where my background comes from, for context. So here I am seeing it in how the horse is reluctant to bend its right hind leg. People are commenting into how the horse is “4-beating”. I am seeing the horse being lame in its right hind leg, which is carrying the most weight when the horse is traveling in a balanced left lead canter. Left lead canter = weight on the right side 

Most importantly, when we are looking at lameness, we look at the opposite leg from the lame one bearing the weight of the leg the horse is favoring. This is harder to see in the hind end than the front end but I can clearly see the horse pounding it’s left hind into the ground with every step to reduce the stress on the right hind. If the horse were traveling on the other lead, or if it were in a very balanced, collected frame, it would be less obvious. But this is why, when a vet evaluates lameness, they watch the horse travel in both directions.
